title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
book_title: Chapter 3: The 300mm Cost Machine — Distribution, Fabs & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: A 300mm wafer has more than double the surface area of a 200mm wafer, yielding roughly 2.3x to 2.5x as many chips at only a fractionally higher processing cost.
epigraph.author: TI Manufacturing Engineering Brief

web_blocks.html: Most analog chipmakers rely on outside distributors like Arrow or Avnet to sell their parts. They also pay outside foundries like TSMC or UMC to make their wafers. Over the past decade, Texas Instruments replaced that model with two linked advantages. First, it built direct-to-customer sales (>80% of revenue) [1, 4]. Second, it scaled internal 300mm wafer fabs [1, 4].

On distribution, TI ended most broad-line distributor deals and moved its 100,000+ buyers onto direct accounts [4]. Those direct accounts run through TI.com and consignment stock programs [4]. Today, over 80% of TI's revenue flows straight from TI to the end customer [4]. Cutting out middleman markups saves several points of gross margin. Even better, TI sees live order flow, sample downloads, and factory demand without distributor lag. To ship fast without distributors, TI holds large internal stock. Inventory reached $4,804 million (222 days) at year-end 2025, then eased to $4.7 billion (194 days) in Q3 2026 [1, 2].

On manufacturing, TI's unit-cost edge comes from wafer size. Most analog rivals still build chips on 150mm or 200mm (8-inch) wafers, often at outside foundries. TI pioneered analog chips on 300mm (12-inch) wafers at RFAB1 in Richardson, Texas [4]. A 300mm wafer has 2.25x the surface area of a 200mm wafer and loses fewer chips at the edge. As a result, each 300mm wafer yields roughly 2.5x as many unpackaged dies. That geometry delivers about 40% lower cost per die and a 20%–40% structural gross-margin edge at scale [4].

web_blocks.takeaway: TI's three 300mm mega-sites (Richardson, Lehi, Sherman) are designed to lift internal wafer fabrication above 95% of total production by 2030 while giving management modular capacity without 3-year greenfield delays.

web_blocks.caption: FY2025 Audited Unit Economics Waterfall ($ Millions, Form 10-K; D&A Separated from GAAP COGS/OpEx)
web_blocks.takeaway: On $17,682M revenue in FY2025, separating $1,918M D&A from GAAP COGS ($7,599M) and OpEx ($4,060M) yields $7,941M Operating EBITDA (44.9%), $6,023M GAAP Operating Profit / EBIT (34.1%), $5,710M PBT (32.3%), and $5,001M GAAP Net Income (28.3%). Operating cash flow reached $7,153M (40.5%), of which $4,550M went to peak-cycle 300mm capex ($2,603M ex-CHIPS FCF; $2,938M incl. $335M CHIPS ITC).

web_blocks.html: Reading FY2025 unit economics requires tracking how depreciation and U.S. CHIPS Act incentives hit the statements [1, 5]. In FY2025, TI booked $1,918 million in depreciation, up from $1,508 million in FY2024 and $1,175 million in FY2023 [1]. That figure was already net of a $353 million cost-of-revenue credit from CHIPS Act incentives [1]. Rising depreciation and startup costs at RFAB2 and SM1 pushed gross margin down to 57.0% in FY2025 [1]. Then revenue jumped from $4,825 million in Q1 2026 to $6,055 million in Q3 2026 [2, 3]. Fixed fab costs spread across far more wafers, lifting gross margin 720 basis points to 64.2% in Q3 2026 [2, 3].

Capital spending is also stepping down sharply. TI spent $5,071 million in 2023, $4,820 million in 2024, and $4,550 million in 2025 to finish the heavy shells at RFAB2, SM1, SM2, and LFAB2 [1, 4, 7]. With those shells in place, management cut FY2026 gross capex guidance to $2.0 billion to $3.0 billion [1, 4, 7]. In Q3 2026, capex was just $463 million, or $2,578 million over the trailing 12 months [2]. TI also locked in $1.6 billion in direct CHIPS Act grants and expects $6 billion to $8 billion in 25% Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) over the buildout's life [4, 5]. Those incentives mean TI's 300mm cost moat is largely built and funded.

Modular Cleanrooms & Long-Life DUV Tooling: Unlike leading-edge logic fabs, TI does not buy $200 million extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) scanners every two years. Its 28nm to 130nm analog and embedded lines run on mature deep-ultraviolet (DUV) tools that stay productive for 15 to 20 years [4]. Because the shells at SM2 and LFAB2 are already built or advancing on schedule, TI no longer faces three-year construction waits [4]. Management can leave cleanroom bays empty until demand justifies adding tools. That turns a lumpy capital plan into a flexible, demand-paced dial.

Assembly, Test & Die-Bank Flexibility: TI's internal reach goes beyond front-end wafer fabs. The company also runs large assembly and test (AT) plants in Malaysia, the Philippines, Mexico, Taiwan, and China [1, 4]. By 2030, TI aims to handle >95% of wafer fabrication and >90% of AT volume inside its own network [1, 4]. Between front-end fabs and final packaging sits an internal die bank. TI stores tested, uncut wafers in nitrogen cabinets before final assembly. When an auto or factory buyer places a rush order on TI.com, TI pulls dies from that bank and ships finished reels in weeks instead of waiting 16 to 26 weeks for an outside foundry [4].

Pulling Foundry Wafers In-House: Shifting wafers from outside foundries into RFAB2, LFAB1, and SM1 delivers a double margin gain. First, TI stops paying the outside foundry's gross-margin markup. Second, each transferred wafer absorbs fixed cleanroom depreciation inside TI's own plants. That dual effect explains why Analog operating margins rebounded to 51.0% in Q3 2026 and why Embedded margins recovered from 11.3% in FY2025 to 26.5% in Q3 2026 [1, 2].

How Direct Consignment & TI.com Cut Working-Capital Friction: Beyond lower die cost, TI's direct distribution system reshapes how buyers manage supply chains [4]. On TI.com, engineers can check live stock, download reference designs, and order production reels with same-day shipping [4, 25]. Large industrial and automotive OEMs also use TI consignment hubs, where TI keeps parts near the buyer's assembly line and books revenue only when parts are pulled. That direct loop removes the double-ordering bullwhip that often distorts distributor channels during chip cycles. It also lets TI plan wafer starts in Richardson, Lehi, and Sherman using real factory consumption rather than distributor guesses [4].

Depreciation Crest & Cash Conversion Beyond 2026: Investors should also track the gap between GAAP accounting depreciation and actual cash upkeep. In FY2025, TI recognized $1,918 million in depreciation, net of a $353 million CHIPS Act offset [1]. That non-cash charge weighed on reported gross margin while new fabs ramped up. Yet once RFAB2 and SM1 reach high load and capex stays in the $2.0 billion to $3.0 billion band, operating cash flow ($7,153 million in FY2025) converts into free cash flow at a much steeper rate [1, 2, 4]. Over a full cycle, 300mm scale plus CHIPS Act tax credits create a durable cash-cost floor that 200mm peers cannot match [4, 5]. That cost floor lets TI defend margins in downturns and compound cash per share in recoveries [4]. As utilization climbs across Richardson, Sherman, and Lehi, every incremental wafer adds high-margin cash flow with minimal extra overhead [2, 4].

web_blocks.title: THE INVENTORY & DEPRECIATION TRADE-OFF
paragraphs: TI's direct model requires holding 180–220+ days of inventory ($4.7B–$4.8B), nearly double the ~110–130 days at distributor-heavy peers. Analog chips rarely spoil—a 10-year shelf life is common—so write-offs stay small. Still, if demand stalls again, $1.9B+ in yearly depreciation and $4.7B of stock tie up cash and widen gross-margin swings.

book_paragraphs: To see why Texas Instruments can price sharply when needed and still earn 50% Analog operating margins, look inside its fabs and shipping docks. Most analog chipmakers act like asset-light designers. They pay outside foundries in Taiwan or Singapore to make wafers, then hand finished chips to distributors like Arrow or Avnet.

Over the last decade, TI walked away from both habits. First, on distribution: TI cut ties with most broad-line distributors and built a direct sales engine around TI.com. Today, over 80% of TI's revenue goes straight to its 100,000+ buyers with no middleman. That saves distributor fees, gives TI live demand data, and lets engineers order parts online at clear prices.

Second, on manufacturing: TI bet its balance sheet on 300-millimeter (12-inch) silicon wafers. Most analog rivals still run on 200-millimeter (8-inch) wafers. Circle math makes the difference clear. A 300mm wafer holds roughly 2.5 times as many unpackaged chips as a 200mm wafer, while processing costs rise only modestly. That geometry yields an estimated 40% lower cost per die.

Let's walk through the FY2025 waterfall to see how every $100 of sales flowed through TI. Out of $17,682 million in revenue, Cost of Revenue took $7,599 million, leaving a 57.0% gross profit of $10,083 million. R&D ($2,083 million), SG&A ($1,860 million), and restructuring charges ($117 million) totaled $4,060 million. That left $6,023 million in operating profit, or 34.1% of sales.

Now look beneath earnings at cash flow. That $7,599 million cost of revenue already included $1,918 million of non-cash depreciation, even after a $353 million CHIPS Act credit. Adding depreciation back, TI generated $7,153 million in operating cash flow—40.5 cents on every sales dollar. In 2025, TI put $4,550 million of that cash straight into 300mm fab construction at Richardson (RFAB2), Sherman (SM1/SM2), and Lehi (LFAB2).

book_subsections.title: Why 2026 Margin & Capex Math Changed So Fast
paragraphs: When you run high-fixed-cost fabs, factory load is everything. In 2024 and 2025, TI paid depreciation and startup costs on half-empty cleanrooms, pulling gross margin down to 57.0%. In 2026, two levers snapped at once. Quarterly sales climbed from $4.83 billion in Q1 to $6.06 billion in Q3, lifting gross margin to 64.2%. At the same time, gross capex dropped from $4.55 billion in 2025 toward $2 billion to $3 billion in 2026, with Q3 capex at just $463 million.

Notice how modular TI's fab plan is from here. Because the structural shells for SM2 in Sherman and LFAB2 in Utah are built or advancing on schedule, TI no longer faces three-year building waits when orders surge. Management can leave cleanroom bays empty until customer demand justifies adding tools. That turns a rigid capital commitment into a flexible dial.

Still, there is a trade-off to respect. To feed an >80% direct channel with fast shipping, TI carries $4.7 billion to $4.8 billion of stock—194 days in Q3 2026, down from 241 days at year-end 2024. Analog chips do not spoil like fresh food, so write-off risk stays low. Even so, that buffer only works if management slows wafer starts when the next slump arrives.

One more operational lever rarely makes the headlines: TI's internal die bank and assembly-test network. Fabless rivals must wait 16 to 26 weeks for an outside foundry to start a wafer from scratch when orders spike. TI stores tested, uncut wafers in nitrogen-purged die banks and runs its own assembly and test plants in Malaysia, the Philippines, Mexico, Taiwan, and China. When a factory or auto buyer places a rush order on TI.com, TI pulls pre-built dies from the bank, packages them in-house, and ships within weeks.

That speed explains why TI's >80% direct channel and 300mm fab network reinforce each other. A direct website without ready stock would lose buyers during shortages. A giant stock buffer without direct demand data would risk building the wrong parts. By owning both the 300mm wafers and the direct buyer link, TI keeps distributor margin, cuts unit die cost by ~40%, and turns inventory into a competitive weapon.

Now look at the U.S. CHIPS Act math inside this buildout. TI secured $1.6 billion in direct CHIPS Act grants plus 25% Investment Tax Credits worth an estimated $6 billion to $8 billion over the life of the Texas and Utah projects. On the income statement, those credits lower yearly depreciation ($353 million in FY2025 alone). On the cash flow statement, they cut cash taxes and capex bills directly. That public co-investment permanently lowers TI's net cost per wafer.

Also watch what happens as TI moves from outside foundries toward >95% internal wafer output by 2030. Every wafer pulled back into RFAB2, LFAB1, or SM1 removes the outside foundry's markup and spreads fixed depreciation over more wafers. That double benefit explains why Analog operating margin snapped back to 51.0% in Q3 2026.

Inside those 300mm cleanrooms, tool longevity matters just as much as wafer size. Logic fabs must spend $200 million per EUV lithography tool every two years. TI's analog and embedded fabs run proven 28-nanometer to 130-nanometer lines on deep-ultraviolet (DUV) tools that last for decades. Once a 300mm stepper or etcher is installed in Richardson or Sherman, it can run for fifteen to twenty years—far past its accounting life. Once the 2023–2025 depreciation wave crests, TI's cash upkeep cost per wafer drops sharply.

Pair that front-end longevity with internal assembly and test plants targeting >90% internal capacity by 2030. TI controls the full physical chain from raw silicon wafer to tested, taped-and-reeled chip. No fabless analog rival can match that vertical control.

Think about what that vertical chain means during a supply crunch or a price war. When a fabless rival wants to cut prices, it still has to pay TSMC or UMC for wafers and pay Arrow or Avnet to distribute the finished reels. Both partners take a cut. TI owns the 300mm wafer line, the assembly and test plant, and the TI.com storefront. That gives TI roughly 20 to 40 percentage points of structural gross-margin headroom at scale.

Just as important is how consignment inventory deepens customer ties. When an auto Tier-1 or industrial OEM links its factory schedule directly to TI's consignment hub, TI sees real assembly-line pull rates every week. That live visibility helps TI keep its own fabs running steadily and prevents the sudden order cancellations that blindside distributor-reliant peers.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The 40% die-cost edge of 300mm wafers is not a slogan. It is simple geometry backed by $14.4 billion of cleanrooms built between 2023 and 2025. As long as TI keeps those fabs well loaded, 200mm rivals cannot match TI's prices without hurting their own margins.
